chunks: From him, from his father, from Abu Talib Abd Allah ibn al-Salt, who said:

Al-Khalil ibn Hashim wrote to the 'Zi al-Ri'asatayn' (the Governor of Two Districts), who was the governor of Naysapur, that a man from the Magians (Zoroastrians) died and bequeathed some of his wealth to the poor. The judge of Naysapur took it and placed it among the poor of the Muslims. Al-Khalil wrote to the Governor about that. The Caliph al-Ma'mun was asked about it and said, 'I have nothing (specific) regarding it.' Then Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) was asked. Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: 'The Magian did not bequeath to the poor of the Muslims, but it is appropriate that the amount of that wealth be taken from the wealth of the Sadaqah (alms-tax) and returned to the poor of the Magians.'

key_terms.أَبَا الْحَسَنِ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ: Abu al-Hasan (Imam al-Rida), peace be upon him
key_terms.ذِي الرِّئَاسَتَيْنِ: Possessor of the Two Authorities/Rank, a title for the governor of Naysapur
key_terms.نَيْسَابُورَ: Naysapur, a major city in Khurasan

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a non-Muslim's bequest to the poor in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the principle of *istihsan* (juridical preference) in Shia fiqh, where Imam al-Rida (AS) prioritizes the deceased's specific intent over a literal interpretation of the bequest's destination. By mandating that the value be deducted from general Muslim *Sadaqah* and returned to the Magian poor, the Imam ensures the bequest remains with the intended demographic, reflecting a nuanced approach to non-Muslims' property rights within the Islamic fiscal system.
